title: DNS Security (DNSSEC) Hashed Authenticated Denial of Existence
summary: Adds the NSEC3 record to DNSSEC as an alternative way to prove that a name does not exist. Unlike NSEC, it uses hashed names to make it harder to list every name in a zone, and it supports opt-out for zones with many delegations. It is a standards-track specification. Later RFCs update it.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5155 defines NSEC3, a DNSSEC method for proving that a requested name or record does not exist. It puts hashed versions of names in the proof chain instead of exposing the names directly, but guesses can still reveal them. An optional setting reduces work for zones with unsigned delegations, at the cost of weaker proof about those delegations.

questions: how does dnssec prove a name does not exist
how to prevent dnssec zone enumeration
how does nsec3 prevent zone walking
what is the nsec3 opt-out flag
subtitle: DNSSEC denial proofs based on hashed names, with an option to omit unsigned delegations from the chain.

tldr.problem: DNSSEC's NSEC records prove that a name is absent by listing neighboring real names. Anyone can follow those records to enumerate a zone, and maintaining proofs for unsigned delegations can be costly.
tldr.mechanism: NSEC3 replaces real names in the denial chain with salted, iterated hashes and defines proofs that validators can check. Its Opt-Out flag lets a chain omit unsigned delegations.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5155 is a Proposed Standard, updated by RFC 6840, RFC 6944, RFC 9077, RFC 9157, RFC 9276 and RFC 9905. NSEC3 makes enumeration harder, but dictionary attacks remain possible, and Opt-Out weakens proof for covered delegations.

today: RFC 5155 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 6840, RFC 6944, RFC 9077, RFC 9157, RFC 9276 and RFC 9905. Read it together with those updates.

sections.title: Why DNSSEC Needs NSEC3
sections.content:
DNS Security Extensions (DNSSEC) use signed records to let a resolver check DNS answers. For an absent name, the original NSEC record identifies two neighboring names and proves that nothing lies between them in the zone's canonical order.

A complete NSEC chain exposes every real name, so anyone can enumerate a zone by making queries. RFC 5155 defines NSEC3 as an alternative: it supports authenticated denial of existence while replacing real owner names in the chain with hashes. It also provides Opt-Out for zones where signing every unsigned delegation would be costly.
sections.plainLanguage: NSEC records can prove that a name is missing, but their chain also reveals all names in a zone. NSEC3 puts hashed names in that chain, making the names harder to discover while preserving signed proofs of absence.

sections.title: Helping Older DNSSEC Resolvers
sections.content:
NSEC3 changes DNSSEC responses, so resolvers that do not understand it might fail to validate a zone. RFC 5155 assigns DNSKEY algorithm identifiers 6 and 7 as aliases for the existing DSA and RSA/SHA-1 algorithms.

A zone using this specification MUST use those alias identifiers for its DNSKEY records. An older resolver sees an unknown algorithm and treats the zone as insecure rather than attempting an NSEC3 validation it cannot perform. A resolver that supports NSEC3 recognizes each alias as its underlying signing algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: The new denial records need resolver support, so RFC 5155 uses special DNSKEY identifiers to signal NSEC3. A resolver that does not know those identifiers treats the zone as insecure instead of trying to validate the unfamiliar proof.

sections.title: NSEC3 Records and Their Parameters
sections.content:
An NSEC3 record lists the record types at one original name and the next hashed owner name in hash order. Together, the records form a circular chain. Each owner name is the base32 encoding of a hash, placed before the zone name. The record also carries the hash algorithm, flags, iteration count, salt, next hash and a bitmap of record types.

The NSEC3PARAM record sits at the zone apex and gives authoritative servers the algorithm, flags, iterations and salt they may use to select a chain for negative answers. Validators and resolvers do not use NSEC3PARAM. Its flags must be zero; a record with nonzero flags is ignored. RFC 5155 assigns record types 50 and 51 to NSEC3 and NSEC3PARAM.
sections.plainLanguage: Each NSEC3 record names a hashed DNS name, lists the record types found there, and points to the next hash in the chain. A separate record at the zone's top name tells authoritative servers which hashing settings to use.

sections.title: Hashing Names with Salt and Iterations
sections.content:
A hash is a fixed-size result calculated from input data. NSEC3 first puts a fully qualified owner name into canonical form: it expands the name, removes compression, and changes uppercase US-ASCII letters to lowercase. It then hashes the name with the salt appended, and repeats the hash using the salt and prior result according to the Iterations field.

The salt makes a precomputed list of likely name hashes less reusable across zones or over time. More iterations make guesses more expensive, but also require more work from authoritative servers and validators. RFC 5155 defines hash algorithm 1 as SHA-1 and limits iteration counts according to the smallest zone-signing key size.
sections.plainLanguage: NSEC3 converts a name to a fixed-size hash after putting it in a standard form. A salt changes the input, and repeating the hash makes guesses slower, but also makes legitimate DNS checks more costly.

sections.title: Opt-Out for Unsigned Delegations
sections.content:
A parent zone can delegate a name to a child zone that has no DNSSEC signature. Without Opt-Out, the parent chain needs a signed NSEC3 record at each delegation to prove whether a DS record exists. When the Opt-Out flag is set, an NSEC3 record may cover one or more such unsigned delegations without a separate record for each.

That lets a zone add or remove unsigned delegations without rebuilding and resigning the chain. An Opt-Out record does not prove whether a covered delegation exists; it still proves facts about other authoritative names. RFC 5155 strongly recommends using Opt-Out sparingly, and says signing tools SHOULD NOT enable it by default.
sections.plainLanguage: Opt-Out lets the signed chain skip individual unsigned delegations, which can reduce the work needed when those delegations change. The skipped names are not proven to exist or not exist, so RFC 5155 recommends using this option sparingly.

sections.title: Building and Checking Denial Proofs
sections.content:
For many negative answers, an authoritative server returns a closest encloser proof. One NSEC3 record matches the closest existing ancestor of the requested name; another covers the next-closer name, showing that the requested name and any intermediate names do not exist. A name-error response also includes a record covering the wildcard name at the closest encloser.

For an answer that has no requested record type, the proof instead shows that the name exists but lacks that type. Validators check the matching and covering records, their type bitmaps and, when needed, the Opt-Out flag. If the next-closer proof relies on Opt-Out, a resolver MUST NOT set the authenticated-data bit because the covered delegation was not cryptographically established.
sections.plainLanguage: A denial proof identifies an existing ancestor and shows that the next name below it is missing. The resolver checks the signed hashes and record-type list; if Opt-Out leaves a delegation uncertain, the answer cannot be marked fully authenticated.

sections.title: Limits on Name Length and Hash Work
sections.content:
Hashed owner names must still fit within DNS's name-length limit. With SHA-1, the hash becomes a 32-character base32 label plus a one-octet length field, so the zone name can be at most 222 octets long.

More iterations increase the cost of guessing names, but also increase the work required to sign zones, answer queries and validate responses. RFC 5155 sets maximum iteration counts based on the smallest zone-signing key: 150 for 1024-bit keys, 500 for 2048-bit keys and 2,500 for 4096-bit keys. A resolver may treat a correctly signed response above the relevant limit as insecure.
sections.plainLanguage: The added hash label reduces how long a zone name can be when SHA-1 is used. Iteration limits balance the extra work imposed on guessers against the work every server and validator must perform.

sections.title: Security Limits and Risks
sections.content:
NSEC3 does not prevent dictionary attacks. An attacker can collect the chain and hash likely names to compare with its entries, although this takes more work than reading an NSEC chain. The RFC says the salt SHOULD be at least 64 bits and unpredictable, and recommends changing it regularly to frustrate precomputed dictionaries.

High iteration counts can create a denial-of-service cost for servers and validators, and a high-count signed record can be used to make a validator treat an answer as insecure. Opt-Out also prevents cryptographic proof of covered unsigned delegations. Walking the chain still reveals the number of records and which record types occur.
sections.plainLanguage: NSEC3 slows attempts to guess names but cannot stop them, and the chain still reveals some facts about a zone. High iteration counts and Opt-Out also have costs or security limits, so the RFC sets limits and recommends careful use.
